Data structure

 Home Computer science
OurBigBook.com Words: 23k Articles: 211
A data structure organizes stored information together with operations for accessing and changing it. Choosing a data structure means choosing which questions should be cheap to answer: an array supports access by numbered position, a hash table supports lookup by key, and a priority queue supports selecting an item by priority. The operations and their time complexity matter as much as the stored values.
Suppose three requests arrive as (5,Ada),(2,Bo),(4,Cy), where the number is a priority and smaller numbers are more urgent. A FIFO queue removes Ada first because she arrived first. A minimum-oriented priority queue removes Bo first because 2 is the least priority. An array can store the same three records in arrival order, but finding the least priority by scanning this representation takes three key inspections. A binary heap organizes these records so the least priority is immediately available. The information is the same; the representation changes the work needed to use it.
This is a useful design principle: preserve just enough organization for the operations the application needs. Maintaining a sorted array gives the whole order, but moving entries to insert a new key can be expensive. A binary heap keeps a weaker heap order that supports fast repeated selection without maintaining a sorted array. A good data structure makes an algorithm's next step easy.

List-based set representation

Words: 44
Data structure OurBigBook.com
Represent a finite set by a list of its elements. Allowing repeated elements makes set union cheap by list concatenation; imposing uniqueness requires membership checks. A representation sorted by a total order and containing no duplicates permits set union and set intersection by a simultaneous scan in linear time. These are different representation invariants for the same abstract set.

Skip list

Words: 54
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A skip list stores an ordered sequence in a bottom linked list, with successively sparser linked lists above it. Searching moves right while the next key is too small, then down a level. Randomly chosen node heights give logarithmic expected search and update time complexity with a suitable height policy. Repeated keys require distinguishing equal-valued nodes by identity when removing their links.

B+ tree

Words: 64 Articles: 1
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A balanced search tree used for database indexes. Records occur at the leaves; internal nodes direct searches using separator keys. A B+ tree with maximum fan-out f has at most f children per internal node.

B+ tree node split

Words: 32
B+ tree OurBigBook.com
An overflowing B+ tree node is replaced by two nodes and a separator is passed to its parent. Splitting the root creates a new root with two children and increases the height by one.

Sentinel value

Words: 26
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A distinguished value marking a boundary or special condition, such as the end of an input sequence. It must be distinguishable from every ordinary data value.

Decimal counter (A∈{0,…,9}k)

Words: 68
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A decimal counter stores a nonnegative integer using an array of base-ten digits, with the least significant digit first. Increment resets trailing nines and increases the next digit, or wraps modulo 10k if all k digits are nines. Starting at zero, the exact number of digit changes in n increments is ∑i=0k−1​⌊n/10i⌋≤10n/9. This is an aggregate analysis proving a constant amortized cost per increment under unit-cost digit updates. An arbitrary initial value contributes an additional O(k) in Big O notation.

Referential integrity

Words: 56
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A constraint requiring stored identifiers or references to denote valid represented entities, except for explicitly permitted absent-reference markers. For a node set T with successor identifiers, integrity can require each nonnull successor identifier to equal the identifier of some node in T. This is separate from identifier uniqueness and from order constraints on values along edges.

Persistent data structure

Words: 260 Articles: 2
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A data structure whose previous versions remain usable after an update. An immutable representation can return a new root while retaining old roots. Persistence is a version-availability property; it does not require copying the whole structure, and it does not by itself guarantee a particular time complexity or space complexity.
Path copying in a balanced tree can preserve old versions while allocating only the updated root-to-leaf path. A linked list can share an unchanged suffix but may copy a long prefix for a positional edit. Retained versions extend the lifetime of their reachable data, which matters when comparing snapshot history with edit-specific inverse commands.

Covariant persistent multiset

Words: 65
Persistent data structure OurBigBook.com
An immutable multiset can expose a covariant type parameter because reading an element only produces that type. Addition accepts a new type parameter with a lower type bound, add[U >: T](x: U), and returns a new ISet[U]. The old ISet[T] retains its contents and original element guarantee. Deletion returns both the removed value and a new remaining multiset; it does not mutate the old one. Duplicate occurrences are preserved.

Structural sharing

Words: 99
Persistent data structure OurBigBook.com
Different immutable versions reuse unchanged component software objects rather than duplicating them. Sharing a linked list suffix or unchanged subtrees saves storage while retaining distinct roots. The shared components must remain immutable for old versions to remain trustworthy. Merely sharing a mutable array does not create a stable snapshot.
Saving references to before/after versions adds constant reference storage per history entry, but the data reachable through those references may be much larger. With balanced-tree path copying, h small updates to a size-n structure can retain O(n+hlogn) nodes. Whole-array copying can instead retain Θ(hn) entries. The implementation and update pattern determine which bound applies.

Optional value

Words: 38
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A value that is either absent or contains one payload. In Haskell, Maybe a uses Nothing for absence and Just x for presence. These alternatives distinguish an absent element from a present payload that may itself be undefined.

Cursor

Words: 38
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A sequential-access object with a non-consuming current-value operation and a separate advance operation. Repeated reads of the current value leave its abstract sequence unchanged. Converting a consuming iterator into a cursor therefore needs a cache or an equivalent saved-current representation.

Iterator

Words: 810 Articles: 11
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A stateful interface exposing a remaining sequence through an availability test and an operation returning and consuming its head. An iterator can represent an infinite sequence without materializing all elements, provided demanded steps terminate. Destructive iterators generally require exclusive ownership of their consumption state; sharing an iterator is not the same as creating a fresh independent traversal.

Bidirectional iterator

Words: 66
Iterator OurBigBook.com
An iterator with forward and backward cursor movement. With the cursor between elements, next crosses and returns the element to the right, and prev crosses and returns the element to the left. Memoizing a forward-only source's consumed prefix supports arbitrary backward travel over that prefix without replaying source effects. The required history storage grows with the farthest explored position, even if the current cursor later moves backward.

Lookahead iterator

Words: 64
Iterator OurBigBook.com
An iterator that physically consumes and caches source elements to determine whether another logical result exists. A prepared optional result makes repeated availability queries idempotent. This is useful when a result requires a complete group of source elements and the underlying iterator exposes neither its remaining length nor a rewind operation. Source consumption is owned by the wrapper; clients must not independently advance the underlying iterator.

Iterator snapshot

Words: 221 Articles: 2
Iterator OurBigBook.com
A new cursor with the same remaining sequence and an independent consumption position. Copying only a wrapper that still points to the same destructive source does not suffice: that gives shared iterator consumption. Cached lookahead and phase flags are part of the state that a snapshot must preserve. Element values need not be deep-copied merely to duplicate the cursor.

Memoized iterator snapshot

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Iterator snapshot OurBigBook.com
Represent a generated sequence by shared memoized lazy list cells and let each iterator hold its own current cell reference. Copy that reference into a new iterator object. Advancing one cursor changes no other cursor, while every cell's future tail is generated once. Thus even a privately stateful generator can supply identical future values to independently consumed snapshots, provided its state is owned by this shared sequence and not mutated externally. Retained older cursors can keep cached prefixes alive. [ref]
Memoized successor chain for stateful iterator copies
Words: 84
Memoized iterator snapshot OurBigBook.com
Represent each generated sequence position by an immutable head and a lazily memoized successor, and give each iterator its own pointer into the shared chain. Computing a successor invokes the privately owned generator once; lagging copies reuse that same successor. Consequently a mutable programming closure generating Fibonacci numbers can support interleaved independent cursor positions. Sharing only the generator and a copied current value would instead consume the generator's mutable state twice. This construction can retain all cells between the fastest and slowest live cursors; it does not guarantee constant memory usage.

Prefix-dropping iterator

Words: 55
Iterator OurBigBook.com
Discard input values until the first one satisfying a predicate, then return that value and every remaining value without testing the predicate again. A demand-driven filtering iterator instead keeps testing and can discard later values too. A buffered first match must survive repeated availability tests and iterator snapshots. A flag distinguishes the initial seeking phase from the already-positioned remainder.

Demand-driven filtering iterator

Words: 117
Iterator OurBigBook.com
An iterator adapter that consumes underlying values only far enough to find the next value passing a predicate. Store at most one passing value in an optional value. With no cached value, its abstract remainder is the filtered underlying remainder; with cached x, it is x followed by that filtered remainder.
Construction performs no read. On hasNext or next, consume rejected values until one passes or the input is exhausted. Cache the passing value immediately and stop. Repeated availability tests reuse it. Returning it clears the cache without prefetching another value. This gives a precise demand boundary even when producing source values is expensive. Availability need not terminate on an infinite input with no further passing value.

Shared iterator consumption

Words: 54
Iterator OurBigBook.com
Two wrappers referring to the same destructive iterator share its remaining sequence. Their local wrapper fields do not duplicate the underlying consumption state. If one wrapper drains the shared source, a later consumer sees exhaustion. Correct reasoning must therefore track aliases and the actual demand order rather than combine the outputs of imagined independent traversals.

Iterator concatenation

Words: 52
Iterator OurBigBook.com
Consume the first iterator until it is exhausted, then consume the second. Short-circuit availability testing avoids polling the second producer while the first still has entries. Construction need not request any entry. If both wrappers share an underlying cursor, however, draining the first may also consume entries the second would otherwise have returned.

Demand-driven alternating iterator

Words: 70
Iterator OurBigBook.com
A wrapper selecting alternate underlying entries can maintain one flag indicating whether the next entry must first be discarded. Construction performs no requests. On demand, skip at most that one entry, clear the flag, and leave the selected entry unconsumed until next is called. Returning a selected entry sets the flag again. Repeated availability tests cannot repeatedly skip; a final skipped entry may need to be consumed to establish exhaustion.

Stateless iterator

Words: 55
Iterator OurBigBook.com
An iterator whose future observable sequence can be produced without changing cursor state. An infinite constant sequence is an example: removing its first element leaves the same sequence. A permanently empty iterator is another. Such cases show why an iterator interface does not logically force every implementing object to be mutable, although ordinary finite nonempty traversals need progress state somewhere.

Occurrence-position representation of a sequence (rep(xs)(v)={i:xsi​=v})

Words: 60
Data structure OurBigBook.com
Represent a sequence by a function mapping each value to its increasing list of occurrence positions. On finite inputs, querying a value produces every matching index and a terminating tail. On infinite inputs, absence of further occurrences may be uncomputable by a generic scan, as expressed by the absence-detection obstruction for infinite lists. Parity filtering and index rescaling represent alternate-element subsequences, but may fail to preserve productivity.

Suffix array (SA)

Words: 123 Articles: 1
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A suffix array stores starting positions of a string's suffixes in lexicographic order. All suffixes starting with a fixed query occupy a consecutive interval. This permits string-searching algorithms to search a compact list of positions instead of storing every suffix explicitly.

Adjacent-suffix characterization of longest repeats

Words: 89
Suffix array OurBigBook.com
The length of a longest repeated substring equals the maximum longest-common-prefix length over adjacent suffixes in lexicographic order. Suffixes beginning with a fixed string form a consecutive interval: a string outside that string prefix software class differs earlier or ends sooner, putting it strictly to one side. Two occurrences of a longest repeated substring therefore bound an interval in which every adjacent pair shares that string prefix. At least one adjacent pair attains its length, and no pair can exceed the global maximum. This proves the result even when occurrences overlap; a text with fewer than two suffixes needs a separate empty-result convention.

Wavelet tree

Words: 42
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A wavelet tree recursively partitions an alphabet and records bit sequences indicating which partition each character belongs to. A character rank query follows the relevant partitions while mapping the prefix length through the bit-sequence ranks. A balanced tree takes logarithmically many levels in the alphabet size.

Rank query (rankc​(r))

Words: 36
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A character rank query asks how many occurrences of character c appear in the first r positions of a sequence. A prefix sum array answers a single-character version in constant time after linear preprocessing; a wavelet tree supports many characters more compactly.

List (abstract data type)

Words: 997 Articles: 15
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A list is an ordered collection in which entries may repeat. Removing duplicates would discard information about both multiplicity and, depending on the representation, order. A linked list and an array are different ways to implement list operations.

Duplicate removal

Words: 155 Articles: 1
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
Replacing a list by a list containing each of its distinct elements once. Retaining first occurrences gives a stable order. A recursive implementation emits the head and removes all its occurrences from the tail before continuing. On an infinite input with only finitely many distinct values, detecting that there are no further new values may diverge; on an infinite input with infinitely many distinct values and terminating equality tests, each successive new value has a finite position and can be emitted.

First-occurrence duplicate removal

Words: 76
Duplicate removal OurBigBook.com
Retain the first occurrence of each distinct value in a list. The right fold foldr (\x ys -> x : filter (/= x) ys) [] preserves this order under lazy evaluation. With terminating equality tests, an infinite input containing infinitely many distinct values produces every finite output prefix. If only finitely many distinct values occur, those values appear but the remaining infinite input cannot generally be certified empty: the result has an undefined tail rather than a terminating empty list.

List reversal

Words: 38
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
Reverse the order of a finite list. Reversal is an involution and satisfies (AB)R=BRAR for list concatenation. In an array segment of length n, exchanging symmetric offsets j and n−1−j for 0≤j<⌊n/2⌋ realizes reversal in constant auxiliary space.

Concatenation tree

Words: 52
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
A tree representation of a list with empty nodes, single-element nodes and binary concatenation nodes. Concatenation constructs one node without traversing either operand. The representation need not be unique: adding empty branches changes its size without changing the denoted list. An accumulator-based traversal gives linear flattening of a binary tree in the representation's size rather than merely the output length.

List zip

Words: 38
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
Combine corresponding entries of two lists into a list of tuples. The usual finite-list operation stops when either input ends. A lazy evaluation implementation can produce entries from infinite lists, but its exact strictness depends on the order of pattern matching in the definition.

Index-function representation of a list (f:Z→Maybe(A))

Words: 67
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
Represent a finite list by a function from indices to optional values. There must be a length m for which exactly the indices 0≤i<m are present; later indices are absent, so the representation has no holes. Prepending and removing a head shift indices, taking restricts the present domain, and dropping translates it. Functional composition can accumulate query costs, so array-like constant-time access does not follow from the representation type.

Random-access list

Words: 204 Articles: 1
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
A persistent list representation supporting positional lookup more efficiently than a conventional linked list. Different implementations trade lookup, insertion and deletion costs; “random-access” does not itself guarantee constant-time indexing. A skew-binary random-access list supports worst-case constant-time front insertion and removal with logarithmic worst-case lookup.

Skew-binary random-access list

Words: 165
Random-access list OurBigBook.com
Represent a finite list by a forest of value-bearing perfect binary trees of sizes 1,3,7,…, in nondecreasing order, using the greedy largest sizes and allowing a repeated size only in the first two positions. Concatenated preorder traversals recover the list. Cached tree sizes guide indexing.
Front insertion merges the first two equal-size trees beneath a new root, or adds a singleton if they differ. Removing the first root either discards a singleton or splits its two children into the initial equal-size pair. Both operations inspect and allocate only a bounded number of constructors, taking worst-case constant time and sharing the remaining representation. A positional query skips whole cached tree sizes and then descends through one tree, taking O(log(n+1)) time. Conversion in either direction takes linear time on finite input.
The duplicate-size restriction follows directly from greediness. If two size-w trees had any preceding nonempty portion, there would be at least 2w+1 elements available, enough for the next larger perfect binary tree. Three equal-size trees would likewise suffice for that larger tree. Both contradict the greedy representation.

Difference list ([a] -> [a])

Words: 160 Articles: 1
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
Represent a list xs by the function \ys -> xs ++ ys. Concatenation becomes function composition, the empty list is represented by id, and applying to [] recovers the list. Only functions of this tail-prepending form are valid representations; arbitrary functions of the displayed type need not satisfy the invariant. A higher-order tree fold using difference lists produces an inorder traversal in linear time on every tree shape.

Linear flattening of a binary tree (go t acc = flatten t ++ acc)

Words: 94
Difference list OurBigBook.com
For a leaf-labelled binary tree, define go (One x) acc = x:acc and go (Two l r) acc = go l (go r acc), then apply go t []. The invariant in the title follows by structural induction and associativity of list concatenation. It proves preservation of leaf order. Each leaf supplies one output constructor and each internal node requires constant bookkeeping, giving linear time in the number of nodes. By contrast, flattening both subtrees and concatenating their results can copy prefixes of sizes 1,2,…,n−1 on a left-branching tree, taking quadratic time. The accumulator is the already-known suffix in a difference list representation.

List concatenation ((++) :: [a] -> [a] -> [a])

Words: 115 Articles: 1
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
Append the second list after the first. For a finite left list of length n, consuming the concatenation costs Θ(n) to copy its spine and can share the second argument. Repeatedly appending large left lists can cause quadratic time complexity; difference lists make concatenation into function composition.

Predicate prefix-suffix reconstruction

Words: 71
List concatenation OurBigBook.com
Concatenating the initial list prefix accepted by a predicate with the remaining list suffix reconstructs the input, provided every test reached before the first false result terminates. Prove the finite case by structural induction: a true test copies the head, and a false test returns the untouched list suffix. An undefined reached test is an obstruction because reconstruction loses an exposed cons cell. An infinite all-true list prefix can still reconstruct the input, since list concatenation never demands its second argument there.

Suffix of a list

Words: 52
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
A list obtained by dropping an initial segment. The whole list and, for finite lists, the empty list are suffixes. Proper suffixes exclude the whole list; nonempty suffixes exclude []. In a linked list, suffixes can share the original nodes, permitting a list of all suffixes to be constructed with linear additional space.

Prefix of a list

Words: 82 Articles: 1
List (abstract data type) OurBigBook.com
An initial segment of a list, including the empty segment and, for finite lists, the whole list. A proper prefix excludes the whole list. Fully materialising all prefixes of a length-n list needs Θ(n2) element constructors, although the outer list of prefixes has only n+1 entries.

String prefix

Words: 35
Prefix of a list OurBigBook.com
An initial segment of a string, including the empty string or the whole string. Two strings share a prefix exactly when their initial characters agree up to its length. The longest common prefix is the longest such shared initial segment.

Heap data structure

Words: 341 Articles: 7
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A tree-based data structure that orders each parent relative to its children so that an extremal value is available at the root. In a max-heap, every parent is at least as large as its children. Heap implementations provide one way to realize a priority queue; the abstract queue and its implementing structure are distinct concepts.

d-ary heap

Words: 147 Articles: 1
Heap data structure OurBigBook.com
A heap data structure stored as a complete rooted tree with up to d children per vertex, where d≥2. The final level is filled from left to right. For zero-based array storage, the parent of entry i>0 is ⌊(i−1)/d⌋, and its child number j∈{0,…,d−1} has index di+j+1 when that index is inside the active heap. There are at most O(1+logd​n) levels containing n entries.

d-ary min-heap

Words: 84
d-ary heap OurBigBook.com
A d-ary heap in which each parent key is no greater than each child key. Transitivity makes the root a minimum. Removing the root requires choosing a smallest child at each downward step, taking O(dlogd​n) time in the usual 2≤d≤n range. Decreasing a key or inserting a new leaf only compares along one chain of parents, taking O(logd​n) time in that range. An array indexed by vertex identifiers can locate each collection; the collection itself may use a linked list or an array. In an undirected graph, each nonloop edge supplies an entry at both endpoints.[ref]
For a worked example, take the simple graph
V={A,B,C,D,E,F},E={AB,AC,BC,CD,DE,DF,EF},
(1)
where AB denotes the unordered pair {A,B}. Its adjacency lists, displayed in label order, are
Adj[A]Adj[D]​=(B,C),=(C,E,F),​Adj[B]Adj[E]​=(A,C),=(D,F),​Adj[C]Adj[F]​=(A,B,D),=(D,E).​
(2)
Thus C has three neighbours, although the graph has six vertices. Its list contains exactly the destinations available for a single step from C; no slots are reserved there for C,E,F. The fourteen neighbour entries represent seven edges, with CD appearing as D in C's list and as C in D's list. The label order makes the example easy to read; an adjacency list need not be sorted.
The useful idea is to store existing connections explicitly. Neighbour enumeration can then follow exactly the possible next steps, which is what breadth-first search and depth-first search need. In a sparse graph, most pairs of vertices have no edge; adjacency lists avoid reserving a separate adjacency matrix entry for every such absence. Whether this saves work depends on the question: neighbour enumeration and testing one proposed edge have different costs.

Orient the seven edges of our example from earlier to later labels. The resulting directed graph has
Adj[A]Adj[D]​=(B,C),=(E,F),​Adj[B]Adj[E]​=(C),=(F),​Adj[C]Adj[F]​=(D),=().​
(3)
There are now seven entries, with outdegrees (2,1,1,2,1,0). In particular, F needs an empty list even though it is reached from D,E: incoming edges do not make F's outgoing list nonempty. Replacing each directed edge by an undirected graph connection would lose this distinction.
Our running simple graph excludes self-loops and repeated edges. If those restrictions are relaxed, specify how the adjacency list encodes them. Here an undirected self-loop at u contributes two copies of u to Adj[u], matching its contribution of two to the degree of a vertex. A directed self-loop contributes one copy, and one each to outdegree and indegree. Distinct parallel edges retain distinct entries; a multigraph's list length can therefore exceed its number of distinct neighbours.[ref][ref]
For example, add one undirected self-loop at A to the seven-edge example. Its list becomes (B,C,A,A), the vertex degree of A becomes four, and the total entry count becomes sixteen for eight edges. If an application instead stores a self-loop once, it must account for its doubled undirected vertex degree separately. In a weighted graph, an entry can be an ordered pair (v,w) meaning destination v and weight w; the weight belongs to the edge, not to the destination vertex.

Adjacency list OurBigBook.com
Neighbour enumeration reports the neighbours of a specified vertex. For a simple graph, scan its adjacency list and report each entry. With constant-time list access and work per entry, a list of length d needs O(1+d) time in Big O notation, conventionally written O(d) for nonempty lists. Use vertex degree for an undirected graph and outdegree for a directed graph. Obtaining the list reference can take constant time; consuming it requires visiting every entry.[ref]
In our undirected example, enumerating C's neighbours reads A,B,D: three entries. Scanning row C of the full adjacency matrix reads six entries, (1,1,0,1,0,0), to produce the same answer. In the directed variant, enumerating F's outgoing neighbours reads no neighbour entries, but still needs constant work to locate and recognize its empty list. For a multigraph, scanning lists enumerates incident edges with multiplicity; reporting only distinct neighbours additionally requires removing repetitions.
For a short time complexity argument, each reported entry requires at least one output operation, and one scan suffices. Across all vertices, the undirected entry count is ∑v∈V​deg(v)=2∣E∣ by the handshaking lemma; the directed count is ∑v∈V​d+(v)=∣E∣. A graph search that processes each vertex once and scans each of its entries once therefore does O(∣V∣+∣E∣) structural work, provided its visited-state access and FIFO queue or stack operations also have the required constant-time costs. With a full adjacency matrix, scanning every row instead inspects ∣V∣2 entries. This is how the representation enters the analysis of breadth-first search and depth-first search.

Adjacency list OurBigBook.com
Write n=∣V∣ and m=∣E∣. Suppose each vertex identifier, list descriptor, link and optional edge weight occupies a constant number of machine words, and indexed array access and identifier comparison take constant time. There are n list descriptors and m directed, or 2m undirected, neighbour entries. Hence adjacency lists use O(n+m) machine words in Big O notation. A full adjacency matrix has n2 entries, regardless of m. These are counts under a storage model, not fixed byte sizes.[ref]
Our undirected example has six list descriptors and fourteen neighbour entries, versus thirty-six full adjacency matrix entries. The numbers 20 and 36 count different kinds of logical items: they do not prove a particular byte saving. A linked list also needs links; an array may have unused capacity. Storing only half of a symmetric matrix changes its exact count while leaving quadratic growth. If identifiers or weights require growing numbers of machine words, their size must be included in the space complexity.
An unsorted adjacency list answers "does the edge u→v exist?" by linear search through Adj[u]. In the worst case it inspects all d entries, giving O(1+d) time, or O(d) for d≥1. Even if v is absent, an uninspected entry could still contain it, so arbitrary lists require the whole scan. On our example, looking for CF in C's list compares F with A,B,D and fails after three comparisons. A full adjacency matrix instead answers from its single C,F entry in O(1) time.[ref]
Different promises change the query. A sorted array of neighbour identifiers permits binary search in O(log(d+1)) time, but maintaining order after insertion may require shifting entries. A per-vertex hash table permits expected constant-time membership under the hashing and load assumptions of that data structure; it does not give that guarantee to an arbitrary adjacency list. A stored list length can likewise make a vertex degree query constant-time even though neighbour enumeration still has to visit its entries.
The advantage grows with scale. For a graph path on n≥2 vertices, m=n−1, so there are 2n−2 undirected neighbour entries and n descriptors, versus n2 full adjacency matrix entries. Such a family is a sparse graph with m=O(n). For a complete graph, m=n(n−1)/2, so the undirected neighbour entries already number n(n−1): the adjacency list advantage in growth rate disappears. Choose by the workload: following existing edges favours adjacency lists; many arbitrary pair-membership queries can favour a full adjacency matrix. The representation organizes the same graph for different questions.

Priority queue

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A priority queue stores items with comparable priority keys and supports insertion, inspection of a best-priority item, and removal of a best-priority item. Here we use the minimum convention: keys have a total order, and smaller means earlier. The operation peek returns a stored item of minimum priority without removing it; extract-min removes and returns such an item. Both require a nonempty priority queue, or an explicitly specified empty-case result. A maximum-oriented priority queue reverses the choice.
For the requests (5,Ada),(2,Bo),(4,Cy), peek returns Bo and leaves all three requests stored. extract-min returns Bo and leaves Ada and Cy; another peek returns Cy. Inserting (1,Dee) now makes Dee the next request selected. This changing collection need not be a sorted array: only the next choice must be available.
Distinct items may share a priority. Inserting (2,Eli) alongside (2,Bo) permits either item to be removed first. A priority queue does not inherently promise arrival order on ties. If that policy matters, compare priority first and a unique increasing arrival number second; the resulting total order makes earlier arrivals win equal-priority ties. This is analogous to the motivation for stable sorting, but it is an extra policy for the priority queue.
The interface specifies behavior; the data structure determines costs. A binary heap implements a priority queue with constant-time peek and logarithmic-time insertion and extract-min, under the cost assumptions below. Scheduling by urgency or by the time of the next event needs exactly this repeated next-item selection. MIT's notes use these applications to motivate the priority queue interface.[ref]

Binary heap

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Priority queue OurBigBook.com
A binary heap represents a priority queue as a complete binary tree obeying a heap order. We use the minimum convention: the priority of every parent in a rooted tree is no greater than the priorities of its children in a rooted tree. Equal priorities are allowed. Each stored entry may be a record carrying a priority key; the numerical example below displays only keys. Reversing the inequalities gives the maximum convention.
The complete binary tree can be stored directly in a zero-indexed array A=(A0​,…,An−1​): read its levels from top to bottom, left to right. The root of a tree is at index 0. The possible children in a rooted tree of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and an index denotes a present entry only when it is less than n. For i>0, its parent in a rooted tree is at ⌊(i−1)/2⌋, using the floor function. Thus the links of the complete binary tree are determined by arithmetic rather than separately stored pointers.
Consider
A=(2,5,3,9,7,8,4).
(4)
The children in a rooted tree of index 0 have keys 5,3; those of index 1 have keys 9,7; those of index 2 have keys 8,4. The six comparisons 2≤5, 2≤3, 5≤9, 5≤7, 3≤8, 3≤4 establish the heap order. At index 4, the parent in a rooted tree is index ⌊(4−1)/2⌋=1, carrying key 5.
The array is visibly not a sorted array: 5 precedes 3, and 8 precedes 4. Nor is the last entry a maximum: it is 4, whereas the maximum is 9 at index 3. The heap order compares ancestors and descendants, without imposing an order between separate branches. Nevertheless, following the graph path from the root of a tree to any entry gives a chain of nondecreasing priorities. This short argument proves that peek can return A0​, a minimum, without inspecting the other entries.
Insertion appends an entry to the array, preserving the shape of the complete binary tree, then uses sift up to repair the heap order. Insert key 1 into the displayed binary heap. It is appended at index 7, and exchanges with indices 3, 1, then 0:
(2,5,3,9,7,8,4,1)​⟶(2,5,3,1,7,8,4,9)⟶(2,1,3,5,7,8,4,9)⟶(1,2,3,5,7,8,4,9).​
(5)
The moving key follows 7→3→1→0; the keys 9,5,2 each move down one level. Only this chain needs repair.
Now apply extract-min. Save key 1, move the last key 9 to the root of a tree, and shorten the array to length 7. Use sift down, always choosing the smaller of the present children in a rooted tree:
(9,2,3,5,7,8,4)​⟶(2,9,3,5,7,8,4)⟶(2,5,3,9,7,8,4).​
(6)
First 9 exchanges with key 2 at index 1, since 2<3; then with key 5 at index 3, since 5<7. At index 3, the possible children in a rooted tree would be indices 7,8, both outside the shortened array, so the process stops. The returned key is 1, and the remaining binary heap is exactly the original one.
For a nonempty binary heap with n entries, the deepest level is ⌊log2​n⌋, using the floor function and logarithm. Each exchange moves one level and uses only a bounded number of comparisons. The resulting time complexity bounds, expressed in Big O notation, are:
OperationTime complexityReason
peekO(1)Read the root of a tree.
InsertO(logn) for n≥2Append, then sift up through at most the levels of the complete binary tree.
extract-minO(logn) for n≥2Move the last entry, then sift down through at most those levels.
Build from an arbitrary arrayO(n)Apply sift down from the last index with children in a rooted tree back to index 0.
These bounds assume constant-cost indexed access, key comparisons and exchanges, and available array capacity for insertion. Allocating and copying a larger array is a separate cost. Empty and one-entry cases take constant work.
To build a binary heap, begin at index ⌊n/2⌋−1 and work backwards. Entries without children in a rooted tree already obey the heap order. Each sift down, also called heapify down, starts with every present smaller rooted tree below it already repaired. Most entries are close to the bottom and can move very little; successively longer repair distances occur for geometrically fewer entries. Summing these distances gives O(n) work, rather than charging O(logn) to every entry. MIT's notes give this bottom-up construction and contrast it with repeated insertion.[ref]
The Dijkstra algorithm additionally needs to decrease the priority of an existing vertex when its tentative distance improves. Given its current index, lowering the key followed by sift up takes O(logn) time for n≥2. An indexed binary heap maintains a separate map from item identity to its current index and updates that map after every exchange. For vertices numbered in a fixed range, the map can be another array, giving constant-time index lookup. An ordinary unindexed binary heap supplies no such guarantee: locating an arbitrary item can require scanning n entries. Item identity and priority must remain distinct, especially when several vertices have equal tentative distances.
The attractive compromise is local organization with global usefulness. A binary heap maintains only the heap order, yet every extract-min gives the next smallest key. Repeated extraction of the original example gives 2,3,4,5,7,8,9, so a priority queue also supplies a sorting algorithm without storing a sorted array between extractions.

After inserting or lowering a key in a minimum-oriented binary heap, compare it with its parent in a rooted tree. Exchange them while the moving key is smaller, then continue at its new index. Hash table

Words: 4k Articles: 16
Data structure OurBigBook.com
A hash table stores records by key: for example, a product number can select its current stock count without scanning every product. A hash function selects a hash bucket in an array, and a collision-handling method such as separate chaining retains distinct keys assigned to the same hash bucket. The useful idea is to narrow the search to one small collection, while key equality decides which record actually matches.
Use a map interface with one value per key: get(k) returns the associated value or an explicit absent result; put(k,v) replaces the value if an equal key is present, otherwise inserts a new record; delete(k) removes the matching record if present. The absent result must be distinguishable from every permitted stored value. Replacing a value does not increase the record count n. A hash collision between unequal keys must never cause one record to replace the other.[ref]
Let x∼y denote the chosen key equality, an equivalence relation, and let hm​ be the bucket-index hash function for m>0 hash buckets. Correctness requires
x∼y ⟹ hm​(x)=hm​(y),hm​(x)∈{0,…,m−1}.
(7)
The converse is false: equal bucket indices merely identify candidates for a key equality comparison. If an implementation first computes a full hash value H(k) and then reduces it to a bucket index, equal keys must have equal H values too. Keep both key equality and the hash function stable while a key is stored; changing the key so it selects another hash bucket can make its record unreachable. This distinction is explicit in the published hashCode/equals contract.[ref]
For a constructed integer example, use modular arithmetic to define hm​(k)=kmodm and store keys 1,5,9,2 with values A,B,C,D. At m=4, three records share hash bucket 1 and one occupies hash bucket 2. The hash table load factor is
α=mn​=44​=1.
(8)
It is the mean number of records per hash bucket, including empty hash buckets, not a bound on the longest chain. With separate chaining, α may exceed 1 because records live in the chains rather than one record being confined to each array slot.
Growing this example to m=8 changes the bucket-index hash function: key 5 now belongs to hash bucket 5, while keys 1,9 still share hash bucket 1. Every record must be assigned using the new bucket-index hash function; copying the old array of chain heads unchanged is insufficient. The hash table load factor becomes 4/8=1/2.
For an insertion-only sequence starting empty with constant initial capacity, one policy doubles m before inserting a new key that would make n>m. A rebuild for separate chaining allocates the new array and transfers each existing record directly into its new chain. Since keys are already distinct, transfer needs no duplicate search. With constant-cost hashing and linking, this takes O(n+m) time complexity, hence O(n) at a growth threshold. Amortized analysis charges the occasional rebuild across many insertions: the old capacities 1,2,4,…,2r form a geometric series with sum 2r+1−1, so total rebuilding work over N insertions is O(N). This gives O(1) amortized resizing overhead; an insertion that triggers a rebuild can still take O(n).[ref]
The search to check for an existing key is additional work. Bounded hash table load factor together with the probabilistic assumptions in separate chaining gives expected amortized O(1) insertion, not worst-case O(1). Rehashing alone gives no distribution guarantee: the diagram's keys 1,9,17,25 all collide modulo both 4 and 8. Even a low hash table load factor permits a long chain. If supporting shrinkage too, leave a gap between growth and shrink thresholds to avoid repeated rebuilding when insertions and deletions alternate near one threshold.[ref]

Separate chaining

Words: 626 Articles: 1
Hash table OurBigBook.com
With separate chaining, each hash bucket in a hash table contains a collection of records, often a linked list. Lookup computes the bucket index, then follows that chain until a key equality comparison succeeds or the chain ends. A hash collision therefore affects the search work without merging unequal keys. Deletion searches the same chain and unlinks the matching record; in a singly linked list, remembering the preceding record during the search permits the unlink.[ref]
For the four-key integer example in hash table, insert a new record at the head of its chain after checking that its key is absent. Inserting (1,A),(5,B),(9,C),(2,D) in that order makes hash bucket 1 hold (9,C)→(5,B)→(1,A), hash bucket 2 hold (2,D), and the other two hash buckets empty. All five subsequent operations below select hash bucket 1 because 5mod4=13mod4=9mod4=1:
get(5) rejects key 9, accepts key 5, and returns B after two key equality comparisons. get(13) rejects 9,5,1 and reports absence after three comparisons. put(5,B*) examines 9,5 and replaces the value without changing n=4. delete(9) examines just the head record, removes it, and gives n=3. Finally, put(13,E) rejects 5,1 before inserting the new head record; n returns to 4 and the chain is (13,E)→(5,B∗)→(1,A). The successive hash table load factors are 1,1,1,3/4,1. These counts follow from the stipulated chain order; a different insertion policy changes the successful-search counts.
For a chain of length ℓ, lookup and deletion by key take O(1+ℓ) time complexity in Big O notation. The same applies to put before any resizing, since replacement semantics require checking for an existing equal key. Head insertion alone is O(1) if absence is already known; that is a different precondition. These bounds assume O(1) bucket-index hashing, array access, key equality comparisons, allocation and link updates. A long string or large integer can make hashing or comparison depend on its encoded length, so counting record visits alone does not establish constant running time.
Under simple uniform hashing, each distinct key's bucket index is an independent random variable with a uniform distribution on a finite set of m indices. The keys and query are fixed independently of this random assignment. Then lookup has expected O(1+α) time complexity, where α=n/m is the hash table load factor; it is expected O(1) when α stays bounded. These are model assumptions, not an automatic consequence of using a deterministic hash function.[ref]
Here is the short calculation. For an absent query q and stored keys k1​,…,kn​, let Ii​ be the indicator random variable of hm​(ki​)=hm​(q). The number C of records inspected has expected value
C=∑i=1n​Ii​,E[C]=∑i=1n​E[Ii​]=mn​=α,
(9)
by linearity of expectation. For a present fixed query, scanning its entire chain inspects at most itself plus all other colliding records, with expected value 1+(n−1)/m; stopping at the match only decreases this upper bound. Adding constant hashing and bucket access yields expected O(1+α) for either query. The argument needs pairwise collision bounds; it does not require all the indicator random variables to be independent. A universal hash family can provide a related bound by random choice of a hash function for a fixed key set, as explained in that article.
The worst case remains O(n), and an absent query takes n comparisons if all n records occupy its hash bucket. For instance, 1,1+m,1+2m,…,1+(n−1)m all collide under hm​(k)=kmodm. Separate chaining remains correct, but a sequence of insertions that each checks the existing chain can take quadratic total work. Amortized analysis of resizing does not remove this search cost, and an adaptive choice of keys based on a known hash function is outside the stated simple uniform hashing model.

Linear probing

Open addressing OurBigBook.com
An open addressing probe rule that visits hm​(k),hm​(k)+1,hm​(k)+2,… modulo m, using modular arithmetic, until a matching record or an appropriate stopping slot is found.[ref]
For capacity m>0, the hash table probe numbered i, starting at zero, inspects the array index
pi​(k)=(hm​(k)+i)modm,0≤i<m.
(10)
The hash function hm​ gives the first array index. Each subsequent hash table probe moves one slot forward, wrapping from m−1 to 0 by modular arithmetic. Keep the hash function and key equality fixed while hash table records are stored.
Use three distinguishable slot states: occupied by a live hash table record; never used since initialization or rebuilding, written E; or deleted, written D, a tombstone in open addressing. Lookup compares occupied hash table keys using key equality, stops at E, and continues past D.[ref]
For an original example, take an eight-slot array, integer hash table keys, and the hash function h8​(k)=kmod8. Start with all slots E and insert the hash table records (0,A),(8,B),(16,C),(9,V) in that order. The insertion hash table probe traces, expressed as array indices, are
016​:0,:0→1→2,​89​:0→1,:1→2→3.​
(11)
The resulting array holds hash table keys 0,8,16,9 at array indices 0,1,2,3, with E in the other four slots. The first three hash table keys have the same initial array index, a hash collision; the fourth begins at 1 but joins the same linear probing cluster. Lookup of 16 examines array indices 0,1,2, rejecting 0,8 before returning C. Lookup of absent 24 examines 0,1,2,3,4, including the stopping E: five hash table probes for a hash table load factor α=4/8=1/2.
Bound lookup to at most m hash table probes, even if no E remains. For algorithm termination, the first m array indices are distinct: equality of pi​(k) and pj​(k) implies that m divides i−j by modular arithmetic, and 0≤i,j<m forces i=j. They therefore cover the entire finite set of slots exactly once. If no occupied hash table key matches and no E is encountered, exhausting these m hash table probes establishes absence; wrapping around again supplies no new information.[ref]
The attraction is a compact array and a simple hash table probe rule. Consecutive slots can benefit from spatial locality, although actual memory cache behavior depends on representation and hardware. Correctness rests on preserving the search route; speed depends on how long that route becomes. The linear probing cluster below explains why even a moderate hash table load factor gives no universal constant lookup bound.
Linear probing cluster

In the eight-slot example, array indices 0,1,2,3 form one linear probing cluster. Inserting absent hash table key 10 starts at 2, passes the occupied slots 2,3, and fills 4. This extends the same linear probing cluster despite 10 having a different initial array index from 0,8,16. A hash collision at the initial slot is enough to make later slots compete too.
For a worst-case family, insert integer hash table keys 0,m,2m,…,(n−1)m into an empty capacity-m array, using the hash function hm​(k)=kmodm, where 1≤n<m. They occupy array indices 0,…,n−1. Lookup of absent nm needs n+1 hash table probes. Taking n=⌊m/2⌋ gives hash table load factor at most 1/2 while the number of hash table probes grows with m. Thus occupancy alone cannot promise constant lookup work.
Before any rebuilding, bounded lookup, deletion by hash table key, and insertion with a duplicate check each have worst-case O(m) time complexity in Big O notation, assuming constant-cost hash function evaluation, array access and key equality. The counterexample gives a matching linear worst-case growth in the number of hash table probes. Hash table resizing is additional work; expensive string comparisons or hashing also fall outside these constant-cost assumptions.

Tombstone in open addressing

Words: 543
Open addressing OurBigBook.com
A deleted-slot marker in open addressing. Lookup continues past it because a hash collision may have displaced a match further along. Linear probing can reuse the slot for insertion after checking for an existing equal key. A genuinely empty slot can terminate lookup; this marker cannot.[ref]
Delete hash table key 8 from the original eight-slot example. Writing E into array index 1 makes lookup of 16 inspect 0,1 and incorrectly report absence, although its hash table record remains at 2. Writing D instead makes lookup pass 1 and reach 2, returning C after three hash table probes. The deleted slot must remember that the search route once continued through it.
A short algorithm correctness proof uses this invariant: no never-used slot precedes a stored hash table key along its linear probing route. Initially the claim is vacuous. Insertion places a new hash table record no later than the first E, possibly at an earlier D, and cannot create an E before another stored hash table record. Replacing a value leaves all slots occupied as before. Deletion to D also creates no E. By mathematical induction over operations, the invariant persists, so stopping lookup at E is sound. Deletion directly to E invalidates that argument, as the diagram shows.
To implement the hash table map operation put(k,v) in one bounded scan, remember the first D encountered, but keep checking occupied hash table keys. A later key equality match means replace that hash table record's value and stop. Only after reaching E, or completing m hash table probes, is absence established. Then insert at the remembered D, if any; otherwise use the stopping E. If all m slots are occupied and no match exists, report full or rebuild before trying again. Merely finding D is not permission to create a second equal hash table key.[ref]
Continue from the correctly deleted example, with hash table keys 0,16,9 at array indices 0,2,3 and D at 1. put(16,Z) examines 0,1,2 and updates the value at 2, leaving 1 deleted and retaining three live hash table records. Inserting immediately at 1 would instead create two copies of 16. Now put(24,W) examines 0,1,2,3,4, proves absence at E, and places the new hash table record at the remembered array index 1. The hash table load factor rises from 3/8 to 4/8; reusing D avoids extending the linear probing cluster to 4.
For a boundary case, fill all eight slots with hash table keys 0,1,…,7 and then delete all eight to D. The live hash table load factor is zero, but absent lookup of 16 still needs eight hash table probes. put(16,C) also checks eight slots before reusing the first D, at array index 0. A loop that waits indefinitely for E would never finish in this state. Rebuilding from the live hash table records into a fresh array removes each tombstone in open addressing and restores never-used stopping slots.[ref]

The collection of records assigned to one bucket index by a hash function. In separate chaining, an array slot refers to this collection, which may be empty.
For m>0 hash buckets, number them 0,…,m−1 and write ℓj​ for the number of records in hash bucket j. Each record belongs to exactly one hash bucket, so

A hash bucket is a destination selected by the bucket-index hash function; with separate chaining, its records need not occupy consecutive positions in computer memory.

Averaging only over nonempty hash buckets gives 12, whereas the hash table load factor is 12/8=1.5. This difference matters when deciding how much array capacity to allocate. Hash table OurBigBook.com
The equivalence relation used to decide whether two keys name the same record. A hash function must respect key equality; a hash collision does not establish key equality.
The choice of key equality is part of the map's meaning. In the one-value-per-key policy of hash table, one record represents each stored equivalence class of keys: put(k,v) updates an existing equal key and adds a record only if no equal key is present. A collection that deliberately retains repeated equal keys has a different policy; its load count must count those extra records too. Repeated calls and distinct stored records are different quantities.[ref]
For an original example, restrict keys to two-letter strings using letters A through Z or a through z. Declare two keys equal when replacing every uppercase letter by its lowercase counterpart gives the same string. Assign each letter its position 1,…,26 in the alphabet, ignoring case, and define the bucket-index hash function as the sum of the two positions modulo 8, using modular arithmetic. Then AB and ab are equal keys and both select hash bucket 3. Key ba also selects hash bucket 3 because 2+1=3, but is unequal to ab: order still matters. Starting empty, put(AB,7), put(ab,9), put(ba,4) leave two records, with values 9 for the ab equivalence class and 4 for ba; the hash table load factor is 2/8=1/4, not 3/8.
The compatibility rule is one-way: x∼y⇒hm​(x)=hm​(y). Otherwise a lookup using an equal spelling could search a different hash bucket and incorrectly report absence. Equal indices merely allow a key equality check. Both the equivalence relation and the hash function must stay consistent while records are stored; changing equality-relevant key contents can invalidate the lookup rule. The Java contract imposes these consistency and equality requirements on equals and hashCode.[ref]

Hash table OurBigBook.com
Changing the number of hash buckets and reassigning stored records using the new bucket-index hash function. Amortized analysis of rebuilding and expected value bounds for subsequent lookup address different costs.

Copying the old eight chain heads and adding eight empty heads would leave those four moved keys unreachable by the new lookup rule.
For a short algorithm correctness outline, allocate the new array, visit every old record once, compute its new bucket index, and link it into that hash bucket. At every step, each transferred record is stored exactly once at the index prescribed by the new hash function. Finishing the visit therefore preserves every key-value association and makes the new lookup rule valid. Direct transfer can skip duplicate searches because the old one-value-per-key map already established distinct equivalence classes; rebuilding is not twelve new user insertions.
Under constant-cost hashing, linking and slot initialization, separate chaining rebuilding takes O(n+m+m′) time complexity: initialize m′ new heads, examine m old heads, and transfer n records. For doubling, m′=2m, this is O(n+m) in Big O notation. It is O(n) when the resize policy makes m proportional to n, but an enormous mostly empty old array can make scanning its heads dominate. Growing capacity can lower α without shortening a particular chain: the concentrated keys 0,16,…,176 all remain in hash bucket 0 after growth from eight to sixteen.

More generally, the transferred old capacities form a geometric series; if the last is M<N, their sum is 2M−m0​<2N. Initializing and scanning these geometrically growing arrays also costs O(N) in total, giving O(1) amortized rebuilding overhead per insertion. A triggering insertion still pays for its whole rebuild.[ref]
The illustrative twelve-record resize above is an explicitly requested rebuild, not a growth triggered by this threshold policy. Checking for an equal key before growing also prevents a value replacement from triggering unnecessary growth. To combine resizing overhead with expected constant insertion time complexity, separately impose the collision and constant-cost assumptions in load factor of a hash table. Amortized analysis distributes rebuilding costs over operations; it does not randomize a poor hash function or bound a single operation's latency. With deletions, separate the grow and shrink thresholds; for example, growing when full and halving at one-quarter live occupancy leaves room for many operations between opposite rebuilds.[ref]

Data structure OurBigBook.com
A FIFO queue is a data structure with first-in, first-out behavior: enqueue inserts at the rear, dequeue removes and returns the front, and peek inspects the front without removing it. A LIFO stack would remove the most recently inserted item instead. A FIFO queue models arrival-order service and supplies the next vertex for breadth-first search; a stochastic service model belongs to queueing theory. [ref]

A linked list with both front and rear pointers supports enqueue, dequeue and peek in O(1) worst-case time under constant-cost pointer operations and allocation, as in Sedgewick and Wayne's implementation. A plain array that deletes its first entry by shifting the remaining n−1 entries takes O(n) time per such removal. An array with advancing front and rear indices can avoid these shifts; storage and resizing policies still need analysis. The two-list functional queue gives a different implementation with constant amortized analysis cost along a single sequence of uses. These representation choices matter when deriving the linear time complexity of breadth-first search in Big O notation.

Binary tree OurBigBook.com
A binary search tree stores key-value entries in a binary tree, with distinct keys drawn from a total order. At every vertex, all keys in its left subtree must be smaller than its own key, and all keys in its right subtree must be larger. Thus the entries represent a partial function from keys to values: a key has at most one associated value and may be absent. [ref]
Lookup starts at the root of a tree. Compare the target with the current key: equality returns its value, a smaller target continues into the left subtree, and a larger target continues into the right subtree. Reaching an empty subtree reports absence. The ordering rule justifies discarding the other subtree at every step; this is the algorithm correctness argument for lookup. It applies to the entire subtree, even if that subtree contains many vertices. [ref]
In the seven-key example, search for 5. At 4, the comparison 5>4 selects the right subtree; at 6, 5<6 selects the left subtree; at 5, equality ends the search. The visited keys are 4→6→5, three key comparisons. The right-child chain stores exactly the same keys and satisfies the same binary search tree rule, but lookup of 5 visits 1→2→3→4→5, five comparisons. Searching for absent key 8 visits 4,6,7 in the first binary search tree and all seven keys in the chain before reaching an empty right subtree.
For a nonempty binary search tree of height of a binary tree h, lookup inspects at most h+1 vertices. Under constant-cost key comparisons and child-reference access, its time complexity is O(h+1) in Big O notation, usually written O(h) for h≥1. With n entries, h≤n−1, giving O(n) worst-case lookup. If the shape is kept balanced so that h=O(logn), lookup takes O(logn) for n≥2. The empty and one-entry cases take constant work. The worst-case linear bound also appears in Sedgewick and Wayne's ordinary, unbalanced implementation. [ref]
In a shape with every level full, there are 1+2+⋯+2h=2h+1−1 vertices, a geometric series. This explains how a small height of a binary tree can accommodate many entries. The binary search tree ordering rule alone does not guarantee this shape or logarithmic time complexity. Breadth-first search also gains no logarithmic key-lookup guarantee merely from having a binary tree: in the displayed balanced example, its left-to-right level order is 4,2,6,1,3,5,7, so it inspects six keys before finding 5, and an absent target requires all seven. Directed lookup uses the total order to choose one branch.
The ordering requirement includes every ancestor on the graph path from the root of a tree. Consider the smaller binary tree with root key 4, left child 2, right child 6, and right child 3 under 2. Key 3 must satisfy both 2<3, from its immediate parent in a rooted tree, and 3<4, from its position in the root's left subtree. Replacing 3 by 5 preserves all immediate parent-child comparisons, including 2<5, but violates 5<4. Lookup for 5 would incorrectly go from 4 to 6 and then to an empty left subtree, overlooking the stored key.
An inorder traversal visits a left subtree, then its own vertex, then a right subtree. On the valid small example its output is 2,3,4,6; on the invalid example it is 2,5,4,6, exposing the descent from 5 to 4. Both seven-key binary search trees yield 1,2,3,4,5,6,7. The theorem is that an inorder traversal of a finite binary search tree with distinct keys lists every key once in strictly increasing total order. For a short proof outline, use mathematical induction on the number of vertices: each smaller subtree produces its own sorted list, and the full ordering rule places every left key before the current key and every right key after it. Concatenating these three parts preserves strict order. Sedgewick and Wayne's keys method uses this left-current-right order. [ref]
This combination is useful and attractive: one data structure supports directed lookup and ordered enumeration. An inorder traversal costs O(n) time complexity for n entries, since it visits every vertex; balance accelerates lookup but cannot eliminate the work of outputting all keys.

    while parent[x] != x:

        parent[x] = root

    return root

def unite(x, y):
    a, b = find(x), find(y)
    if a == b:
        return False
    if rank[a] < rank[b]:
        a, b = b, a
    parent[b] = a
    if rank[a] == rank[b]:
        rank[a] += 1
    return True
Starting from the displayed disjoint-set forest, find(3) traverses 3→4→2, returns 2 and changes only parent[3] from 4 to 2. The route 5→6→2 still has two edges. Then find(5) changes only parent[5] from 6 to 2. The final parent array is (2,2,2,2,2,2,7); every stored rank retains its displayed value. The rooted tree at 2 now has height one although its root's rank is two. Root 7 still represents a separate singleton set.
The two-pass algorithm first discovers the answer and then reuses it. During the second pass, saving following before overwriting the pointer preserves the remaining route. Every replacement pointer targets the original root of a tree, proving that the partition of a set is unchanged.
Full path compression is one specific rule. The authored UF.java implementation instead uses path halving, redirecting a visited member to its parent's parent while advancing along the route. Its union by rank rule agrees with the one above.[ref]

Union-find operation bounds (O(n+mα(n)))

Words: 335
Disjoint-set data structure OurBigBook.com
Assume identifiers, pointers and ranks fit into constant-size machine words, with constant-cost indexed array access, comparison and assignment. Initializing n≥1 members costs O(n) time and machine words. With union by rank and full path compression, any sequence of m disjoint-set find operations and disjoint-set union operations then has total time complexity, in Big O notation,
O(n+mα(n)).
(26)
Here α(n)≥1 is a conventionally normalized inverse Ackermann function. The documented path-halving implementation has the same amortized analysis bound.[ref]
A disjoint-set union operation includes two disjoint-set find operations and a constant amount of additional linking work. Including n in the bound accounts for initialization even if no queries follow.
This is a bound on an entire sequence. It is not a worst-case constant bound for each call: a disjoint-set find operation can still encounter a previously uncompressed route of logarithmic length. The inverse Ackermann function grows extraordinarily slowly but is unbounded, so it cannot be replaced by a mathematical constant in this asymptotic statement. The general distinction between a per-operation maximum and a whole-sequence guarantee is explained in amortized analysis.
Robert Tarjan's 1975 paper established an inverse Ackermann function bound for set union. Its abstract states the sharper two-parameter form for m≥n representative queries and n−1 intermixed merges: the worst total cost is bounded above and below by positive constant multiples of mα(m,n). Those variables count different operations from the convenient n+mα(n) formulation above; the abstract's matching lower bound is about its analyzed method, rather than a claim that every conceivable representation obeys the same lower bound.[ref]
The intuition is that union by rank limits how parent routes grow, while path compression makes an expensive traversal improve later queries. The rank argument alone proves only a logarithmic bound. Establishing the inverse Ackermann function bound requires a finer accounting of traversals across rank ranges; it does not follow merely from drawing a flatter rooted tree. The useful result is that repeated merging and membership queries can share the work of maintaining a changing partition of a set.
